title: Poulet Rôti
subtitle: French roast chicken with butter, garlic, and tarragon
excerpt: A whole chicken rubbed with butter and tarragon and roasted at high heat. The technique produces crisp, golden skin and juicy meat, with a brief resting time to redistribute the juices before carving.
sourceNotes: Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), poulet rôti entry. Thomas Keller's methods for resting and seasoning chicken, widely referenced in French-derived roasting technique. The butter-and-tarragon treatment is standard in French domestic roasting guides from the mid-20th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Season and butter the chicken the night before and refrigerate uncovered. The skin dries out slightly in the fridge, which helps it crisp during roasting.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving cooked meat to stand off the heat before carving. The internal temperature continues to rise slightly and the juices redistribute through the meat, making each slice more moist.

content.text: Poulet rôti is a whole chicken roasted in a hot oven until the skin is golden and crackled, the meat cooked through to the bone, and the resting juices puddled in the pan. It is the French version of a dish every culture has: a whole bird, high heat, the simplest possible seasoning. The French habit of adding butter under and over the skin and using tarragon keeps the meat moist and gives the skin a gloss.
A 1.6 kg bird at 220°C takes about 1 hour 10 minutes. The internal temperature at the thickest part of the thigh (away from the bone) should reach 75°C.
for 15 minutes is not optional; cutting straight from the oven sends all the juices to the board rather than the plate.

items.prepNote: about 1.6 kg, at room temperature for 30 minutes before roasting
leaves picked, plus extra sprigs for the cavity

content.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (190°C fan). Mix the soft butter with the tarragon leaves and a generous pinch of salt and pepper. Loosen the skin over the breast with your fingers, starting at the neck end, working in a pocket between the skin and flesh without tearing the skin. Push most of the butter under the skin and spread it evenly over both breasts. Rub the remaining butter over the skin.
Season the cavity generously. Tuck the garlic cloves and a few tarragon sprigs into the cavity. If using, add the lemon halves. Truss the legs loosely if you like, or leave them untied.
Place the chicken breast-side up in the roasting pan. Roast at 220°C for 20 minutes until the skin starts to colour.
Reduce the oven to 190°C (170°C fan). Roast for a further 50 minutes, basting once halfway through with the pan juices.
Test the chicken: pierce the thigh at its thickest point. The juices should run clear, with no pink. An instant-read thermometer should read 75°C.
Tip the pan so the juices inside the cavity run into the roasting pan. Rest the chicken for 15 minutes, loosely covered with foil, before carving.

items.symptom: The skin is golden but the thigh meat is still pink
items.cause: The oven temperature was too high and the outside cooked faster than the inside.
items.fix: Return the chicken to a 180°C oven for 10 to 15 minutes. If the skin is at risk of burning, cover loosely with foil. The skin can always be re-crisped briefly under a hot grill at the end.

items.symptom: The skin is pale and soft, not crisp
items.cause: The oven was too cool, or the chicken was wet when it went in.
items.fix: Blot the chicken thoroughly dry before buttering next time. If the skin is soft after roasting, slide the bird under a hot grill for 4 to 5 minutes, watching closely.

items.symptom: The butter burns in the pan
items.cause: The oven temperature was very high and the pan ran dry.
items.fix: Add a splash of water or chicken stock to the roasting pan at the start of cooking to create some steam and prevent the drippings from scorching.

items.cause: The chicken was overcooked or rested for too long with the foil tight against the skin.
items.fix: Rest loosely covered, not wrapped tightly. Use a thermometer: 75°C at the thigh is the target. Beyond that, the breast meat dries quickly.

content.text: The French roast chicken is deeply embedded in daily cooking. Rôtisserie shops selling only poulet rôti appear in most French market towns and city neighbourhoods. The stall with turning chickens and a tray of potatoes basting below in the dripping is a fixture of French street markets. The phrase "il tourne comme un poulet" (he spins like a chicken) has passed into everyday speech. The Bresse chicken (poulet de Bresse) holds an AOC designation and is considered the finest table bird in France. It is distinguished by white feathers, blue feet, and a red crest, and is raised to strict standards in the Ain department.
